name: Tundra Yukaghir
confidence_why: Schmalz (2013), the reference grammar, describes Tundra Yukaghir stress as non-phonemic and 'a controversial topic', with Krejnovič (1968, 1982) placing it freely on the first, second or any syllable, Nikolaeva (2002) proposing a rightmost-heavy-syllable rule, and Odé reporting that speakers themselves disagree on whether word stress exists, so no placement can be defended until the promised experimental study appears.
catalog_citation: Schmalz, Mark. 2013. Aspects of the grammar of Tundra Yukaghir. PhD dissertation, Universiteit van Amsterdam, ix+370 pp. (UvA-DARE hdl 11245/1.400358; open PDFhttps://pure.uva.nl/ws/files/1518096/130869_thesis.pdf)
catalog_locator: sec. 2.6.1 'Stress', p.59 (the TOC prints 58), incl. footnotes 85-86; summary sentence p.352.
catalog_quote: TY has non-phonemic free stress, that is, stress is not fixed on one syllable for each word, and there are no minimal word pairs on the basis of stress position. [...] However, for TY no such regularities have been experimentally verified yet, which is reflected in the diverging conclusions scholars have drawn while studying this issue, as is presented below. Krejnovič (1968:437) is very brief, stating that stress is free in TY and can lie on the first or second syllable. Krejnovič (1982:19) modifies his view by saying that any syllable can be stressed and adds that inflectional suffixes attract stress. [...] Nikolaeva (2002:11) provides a concise description of stress assignment rules for TY. She establishes the following stress attracting hierarchy: rightmost V1V2/V: > rightmost CVC > rightmost CEC > rightmost open syllable. An important stipulation is that syllable with the structure CE cannot bear stress. Odé (personal communication) reports that speakers of TY have different opinions regarding the existence of lexical stress and its assignment rules. [...] [p.352] Stress is a controversial topic. Some syllables do seem to have a measurable prominence compared to others, however no decisive answer could be proposed to explain the regularities of stress assignment. Stress appears to be phonologically irrelevant.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (383 pp., UvA-DARE 'Final published version' cover sheet on p.1; extracted text copy). p.72 carries the running head '59' at top right and contains sec. 2.6 Suprasegmentals / 2.6.1 Stress (the text; 71 form-feeds precede the section, so PDF page 72; the TOC line 144 prints '2.6.1 Stress 58'). Every sentence of the reported quote is on that page word for word, in the order given, with the [..] elisions correctly marking the omitted sentences ('In languages with lexical word stress.. length and intensity.' and the Kurilov 2006:38 sentence); the page render shows the same text and the page number 59. Footnotes 85 (Jochelson 1905:374-375 = KY, not reported) and 86 (E = reduced vowel afte…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Schmalz's own position: stress is non-phonemic and 'free' (not fixed to a syllable, no minimal pairs), no phonetic correlate verified, and 'appears to be phonologically irrelevant' (p.352). The only explicit placement rule he reports is Nikolaeva's (2002, unpublished): stress goes to the rightmost heavy syllable, weight ranked long vowel/diphthong > closed CVC > closed syllable with reduced vowel (CEC) > rightmost open syllable, and a syllable with a reduced vowel (CE) never bears stress. That is a weight-sensitive right-edge rule, and it matches the rule Nikolaeva & Xelimskij 1997:157 give for Yukaghir generally (last heavy syllable = long vowel or CVC, else the final syllable), whose examples are however Kolyma words. Krejnovič's earlier statements (first or second syllable; any syllable, suffixes attract stress) conflict with this. If a catalog reading has to be chosen, weight-sensitive (rightmost heavy, else final) per Nikolaeva is the only formulated rule; Schmalz himself declines to endorse it.
new_statements.exceptions: Nikolaeva's stipulation that CE (reduced-vowel) syllables cannot bear stress; Krejnovič 1982's remark that inflectional suffixes attract stress; Odé (p.c.) reports speakers disagree about whether lexical stress exists at all. Footnote 85: Jochelson 1905:374-375 describes Kolyma, not Tundra, stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (word forms in isolation); Schmalz treats intonation separately in 2.6.2 (polarity questions: pitch rise on the penultimate syllable of the predicate, half fall on the last). Matić & Odé 2015 show focus is signalled by pitch movements at phrase level.
new_statements.identity_note: Schmalz 2013 describes Tundra Yukaghir (= Northern Yukaghir, nort2745, ISO ykg) on the basis of 2009-2012 fieldwork in Andrjuškino, Lower Kolyma. The other statement held by the project (Nikolaeva & Xelimskij 1997, p.157) is a joint 'Jukagirskij jazyk' chapter whose description is explicitly based on the Kolyma dialect (sout2750) with Tundra data flagged only where marked, and the stress examples are Kolyma words; it therefore supports but does not itself state the TY rule. NB: an earlier compilation named source 'Nikolaeva 2014, A Grammar of Tundra Yukaghir (Mouton)' does not exist: DOI 10.1515/9783110320640 is Nikolaeva 2014 A Grammar of Tundra NENETS. A Grammar of Tundra Yukaghir by Dejan Matić & Irina Nikolaeva (De Gruyter Mouton, ISBN 9783112259337) is listed by Google Books with publication date 2026-10-05, i.e. forthcoming.

sources.tag: read: notes on stress
sources.note: p.156 sec.2.0.0: description based on the Kolyma dialect, Tundra data flagged specially. p.157 sec.2.1.2: no tonal contrasts; stress is mobile (raznomestnoe), non-distinctive, structure-dependent: falls on the last heavy syllable (long vowel or closed CVC) of the word form, otherwise on the final syllable; examples are Kolyma words (šoromə́ 'person', jel'ṓd'ə 'sun'). Not marked as Tundra-specific; same hierarchy Schmalz attributes to Nikolaeva 2002 for TY.
